item.title: Hijacked Optimizely Scripts Served Card Skimmer and iOS Exploit Kits to CNN, BBC and Zoom Visitors
item.description: An attacker exploited a flaw in Optimizely Web Experimentation to plant malicious code in some of the scripts that customers' websites load from the service, Optimizely said early today. Visitors to sites run by at least 178 organizations, including CNN, the BBC and Zoom, received the code yesterday, according to Report URI, a firm that monitors the scripts websites run. The code was built to replace crypto wallet addresses with the attacker's own addresses and to capture card details, but the firm cannot see how many card numbers were exposed to the attacker. The vendor says it has fixed the flaw and removed the code. On iPhones and iPads, the code was also set up to load a second stage that the firm identifies as an iOS exploit kit, but it reports no iPhones actually being taken over. In an incident notice posted at 01:02 UTC, Optimizely said the attacker had "exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation" and used it to add malicious JavaScript to some cus...

item.description: ConnectWise on Monday said it completed its investigation into unauthorized access targeting partner ScreenConnect environments, and recommended customers to ensure that the technician client is running version 26.6.5 or later. The company said additional activity targeting on-premises environments continues to be reported where the identified third-party extensions remain enabled, and ScreenConnect has not been updated to the latest version. "On-premises partners must immediately disable the identified extensions and update ScreenConnect to the latest supported version," the company said . It's worth noting that version 26.6.5 addresses a critical-severity flaw in ScreenConnect client tracked as CVE-2026-84869 (CVSS score: 9.9) that could allow files to be transferred and executed through an active remote session without authorization or Host confirmation in certain circumstances. item.description: N-able has released a new security update to address additional critical security flaws impacting N-central. Describing N-central 2026.4 Hotfix 3 as a critical security update, the company said it includes a number of security patches and fixes that enhance the security of the Remote Monitoring and Management (RMM) and Unified Endpoint Management (UEM) platform. "HF3 builds on the protections delivered in HF2 and includes further improvements across authentication and access controls, Agent and Probe communications, file handling, server components, legacy APIs, and user management," the company said . The improvements relate to authentication and access control; Agent, Probe, and appliance security; file and import handling; server hardening; and user management controls. item.title: Google Finds Hackers Using AI Agents to Build and Run Exploits From Software Patches
item.description: Google on Monday revealed that adversarial use of artificial intelligence (AI) by threat actors has gone beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks like ARTEX, CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. In tandem, threat actors are leveraging the power and capabilities of large language models (LLMs) and agentic frameworks to automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize newly disclosed vulnerabilities, as observed in the case of PaperCut NG/MF flaws earlier this September. The abuse of open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks is seen as a way to "automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions," Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) said in a report shared with The Hacker News. The tech giant said the adoption represents a paradigm shift in which cyber a...

item.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: N-able 0-Days, Windows 0-Days, Chrome 0-Days, Fridge 0-Days, and More Bad Days
item.description: A default password opened doors it never should have. A trusted update delivered malware. Even a security feature became a way to break in. Different stories, same problem: the things meant to protect us aren't always doing their job. Meanwhile, AI is making bug hunting faster, old flaws are still paying off, and attackers keep finding easy ways in. Some attacks take real skill. Others barely need any. This week's stories show both sides. Here's what happened. ⚡ Threat of the Week N-able 0-Days Exploited for Dropping Crypto Miners — A new set of vulnerabilities tracked as 4EverAble2Shell has come under active exploitation, with attackers exploiting it to deploy cryptocurrency miners on vulnerable servers. According to Huntback, the activity has successfully compromised 21 N-central servers across the U.S., South Africa, Canada, the U.K., Germany, France, and Sweden. Patches for the flaw are expected to be released N-able today.

item.title: Six Unpatched Danfoss Refrigeration Controller Flaws Could Allow Remote Takeover Without Login
item.description: Six flaws in Danfoss AK-SM800A refrigeration controllers could let a remote attacker take over a controller without logging in, Dutch security consultancy Midnight Blue said earlier this week. No patch is available, and the researchers say the newest firmware, version 5.4.0, does not fix the flaws. Government cybersecurity agencies in Belgium, Ireland and Germany told operators this week to take the controllers' management interfaces off the internet. For a controller left on the internet, updating the firmware, changing default passwords or turning on Strict mode is not enough on its own, the Belgian and Irish agencies said. Strict mode is a login protection that requires encrypted connections and session tokens, but one of the six flaws is in the gateway that enforces it. The AK-SM800A runs a store's fridges and freezers, and maintenance firms can manage it remotely. Such controllers were targeted in attacks in France starting October 11, and in a second wave acros...

item.title: Retadup Worm Resurfaces 7 Years After Takedown to Spread CoffeeLoader Malware
item.description: Cybersecurity researchers have disclosed details of a new variant of CoffeeLoader , a malware designed to deliver additional payloads to infected machines. "On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named '7z.dll' into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe," Kaspersky said in an analysis published today. "The '7z.dll' file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer." CoffeeLoader was first documented by Zscaler ThreatLabz in March 2025, detailing its use of the Armoury packer to resist analysis and ultimately run Rhadamanthys shellcode. item.title: SANSAR Linux Cryptomining Malware Uses Modified NVIDIA Library to Hide GPU Activity
item.description: A financially motivated threat activity cluster tracked as REF3364 has been attributed to a Linux-focused cryptocurrency mining operation that tampers with the readings used to detect high GPU workloads. Central to the intrusion is a toolkit called SANSAR , a Rust-based orchestrator that receives commands over the TOR anonymity network to manage CPU and GPU miners. The activity was observed in late October 2026. "The threat actor also deployed a kernel rootkit to hide selected processes and files, an NVIDIA Management Library ( NVML ) wrapper to falsify GPU readings, and a separate backdoor named netns," Elastic Security Labs said in a report published last week. "This backdoor retrieves its C2 [command-and-control] address from an Ethereum smart contract before connecting to the server directly." item.title: Amazon Uncovers AI Agent Campaign Targeting LiteLLM, Dify, and Other Apps for API Keys
item.description: Attackers' AI agents have been hunting for weak spots in internet-exposed AI apps such as LiteLLM , One API , and Dify to steal the AI provider keys stored inside, according to the agents' own records. The records, which Amazon's threat intelligence team captured with decoy servers, describe stolen keys being used to run the AI models that powered the search for more keys. The team said this week that it cannot verify the outcomes reported by the agents. It has moderate confidence that the agents ran on ARTEX , an open-source AI tool for penetration testing. The records include a playbook of known entry points for each targeted product. It lists default administrator credentials such as LiteLLM's default master key, unfinished installs that an outsider could take over, and known flaws in Langflow and RAGFlow . item.title: BO Team Exploits Log4Shell in VMware vCenter, Compromises Russian Firm's Code-Signing Server
item.description: An investigation into suspicious activity within a Russian software developer's network has uncovered a months-long compromise of its development infrastructure and a software code-signing server. The activity, documented by Kaspersky's ICS CERT team after it was contacted by the affected developer in June 2025, has been attributed to a threat actor named BO Team (aka Black Owl, Hoody Hyena, and Lifting Zmiy). The name of the targeted company was not disclosed, but it operates from within Russia and develops software that has a "customer base in the Russian Federation," according to Kaspersky. Over the course of several months, the intrusion resulted in the theft of confidential information and the compromise of all components of the organization's IT infrastructure, including Windows and Linux servers, workstations, hypervisors, backup servers, security solution management servers, and network equipment.
